research_text:
## Factual research brief — `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` / `SSLContextSpec`

### 1. What `SSLContext` governs, and what the finding refers to

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation. It acts as a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances, and is initialized with optional key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source. `SSLContext` is part of JSSE, whose purpose includes TLS/DTLS encryption, authentication, and integrity protection. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The reported message — *“the observed call sequence is not one SSLContextSpec accepts”* — is **not a Java API exception or a TLS-handshake result**. It refers to the call-order/property language in the cited CrySL specification:

- required order: `Get, Init, Engine?`;
- forbidden event: `getDefault() => Get`;
- a constraint on the `protocol` variable: only `"TLSv1.2"` or `"TLSv1.3"`;
- required analysis predicates for the three `init` arguments: `generatedKeyManagers[km]`, `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`, and `randomized[random]`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

Thus, this kind of finding is about the rule’s modeled **API-event trace and rule predicates**, rather than evidence of the actually enabled protocols, negotiated protocol, certificate-validation outcome, hostname-verification outcome, or live runtime behavior. The rule has no events for configuring enabled protocols through `SSLParameters`, `SSLSocket`, or an `SSLEngine`, nor for handshaking. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

In particular, the Java standard names specification says that `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` means “supports some version of TLS” and may support other SSL/TLS versions; `"TLSv1.2"` and `"TLSv1.3"` similarly may support other SSL/TLS versions. Therefore, neither the requested `SSLContext` name nor the CrySL literal check alone establishes what protocol will be enabled or negotiated. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html))

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation guidance

#### Documented API lifecycle

The official Java API documents these relevant behaviors:

1. **Create an `SSLContext`** with one of the `getInstance` overloads and a standard protocol name. Provider selection is either provider-list based, provider-name based, or explicit-provider based, depending on the overload used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))  
2. **Initialize a newly created context** with `init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)`. The API documents that either manager array may be `null`; in that case, installed providers are searched for an appropriate highest-priority factory implementation. A `null` random argument selects the default implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))  
3. **Obtain factories or create an engine after initialization.** `getSocketFactory`, `getServerSocketFactory`, and `createSSLEngine` document `IllegalStateException` when the provider requires initialization and `init()` has not been called. The `SSLEngine` documentation likewise says it is created from an initialized `SSLContext`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))  
4. **Configure connection-level settings before the handshake.** `SSLParameters` holds allowed protocol lists, cipher suites, endpoint identification, SNI, client-authentication settings, and other connection parameters, and can be applied to sockets or engines. The `SSLEngine` documentation says engine-specific settings should be set before the first `wrap`, `unwrap`, or `beginHandshake`, which trigger the initial handshake. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html))  
5. For an `SSLEngine`, the API specifically recommends explicitly setting client/server mode with `setUseClientMode()` because the default is provider-specific. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

#### Trust and authentication

The JSSE reference guide identifies a `TrustManager` as responsible for deciding whether presented authentication credentials are trusted; untrusted credentials terminate the connection. It says a `TrustManager` may be provided explicitly, or, when `null` is passed to `SSLContext.init`, one is obtained through the provider mechanism. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

Accordingly, the official sources support retaining normal trust-manager based certificate decisions and connection-level endpoint identification as applicable. They do **not** describe disabling certificate validation or hostname/endpoint identification as a remediation for an `SSLContext` sequence finding. `SSLParameters` explicitly includes an endpoint-identification-algorithm parameter. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html))

#### `getDefault()` is API-valid but CrySL-forbidden

The Java API documents `SSLContext.getDefault()` as returning the default context; if no default was set, the first call creates it via `SSLContext.getInstance("Default")`. The resulting default context is immediately usable and does not require initialization. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

That API-valid behavior conflicts with this particular CrySL source, which expressly lists `getDefault() => Get` under `FORBIDDEN`. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Recommended remediation: source limitation

Neither the `SSLContext` API documentation nor the JSSE reference guide provides a remediation procedure for a **CrySL/CogniCrypt `SSLContextSpec` violation**. The Java documentation describes API semantics, initialization requirements, provider behavior, and connection configuration; it does not prescribe how to make a third-party static-analysis rule accept a trace.

The rule source itself specifies the accepted order, literal protocol constraint, forbidden event, and predicates, but it does not contain an explanatory migration/remediation section. Consequently, a rule-specific remediation recommendation cannot be attributed to the official Java sources or to this CrySL file alone. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

### 3. Compatibility, formats, version support, and migration

#### Persisted formats

The examined `SSLContext` API and JSSE reference materials do **not** define an `SSLContext` persisted-data format or a persisted `SSLContext` configuration format. The documentation describes a runtime context initialized from managers and a random source; it does not document persistence or conversion of an `SSLContext` object. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

#### Wire formats and interoperability

JSSE/TLS uses a handshake to establish connection parameters. `SSLParameters` exposes the list of protocols allowed for a connection, and the standard names specification says a context requested with a particular protocol name may support other SSL/TLS versions. The supported/enabled/negotiated values therefore remain distinct concepts in the official documentation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html))

The CrySL condition is narrower: it checks the `getInstance` argument against two exact strings. It does not document wire-format migration, peer interoperability, enabled protocol configuration, or negotiated-protocol verification. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Java platform support

`SSLContext` itself has existed since Java 1.4; `createSSLEngine` is since Java 1.5; `getDefault`, `setDefault`, and default/supported SSL-parameter accessors are since Java 1.6. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Version support for named TLS contexts is release- and provider-dependent:

- Current Java SE 25 API documentation says every Java-platform implementation must support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
- Java SE 8 API documentation only required `TLSv1`; it directs users to implementation release documentation for other supported algorithms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle’s Java 8 JSSE guide identifies TLS 1.3 support in the SunJSSE `SSLContext` table as beginning with JDK 8u261. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/technotes/guides/security/jsse/JSSERefGuide.html?utm_source=openai))

Therefore, a portability claim for `"TLSv1.3"` cannot be made without the actual target JDK release and provider. The current specification’s mandatory-support statement does not retroactively establish support in older Java runtimes. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

#### Documented migration path

No examined official source specifies a migration path from one `SSLContext.getInstance` protocol string to another, nor any persisted-format or wire-format conversion procedure. The Java guidance is instead to use standard names and consult the implementation’s release documentation for supported algorithms. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

### 4. Exact matching rule in `SSLContext.crysl`

**Primary rule source:**  
`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl`

The source scopes the rule to this API type:

> `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`

It declares these typed objects:

> `java.lang.String protocol;`  
> `javax.net.ssl.KeyManager[] km;`  
> `javax.net.ssl.TrustManager[] tm;`  
> `javax.net.ssl.SSLEngine eng;`  
> `java.security.SecureRandom random;`

The full event-matching clause is:

> `g1: getInstance(protocol);`  
> `g2: getInstance(protocol, _);`  
> `Get := g1 | g2;`  
>   
> `i1: init(km, tm, random);`  
> `Init := i1;`  
>   
> `se1: eng = createSSLEngine();`  
> `se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_, _);`  
> `Engine := se1 | se2;`

The source’s forbidden clause is:

> `getDefault() => Get;`

The order clause is:

> `Get, Init, Engine?`

The condition directly evaluated for the protocol variable is:

> `protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};`

The source additionally requires:

> `generatedKeyManagers[km];`  
> `generatedTrustManagers[tm];`  
> `randomized[random];`

And it ensures:

> `generatedSSLContext[this] after Init;`  
> `generatedSSLEngine[eng] after Engine;`  
> ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

#### Match scope and parameter constraints

- **Receiver/API type:** The specification is explicitly declared for `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. The event lines do not separately repeat a receiver type; that type is supplied by the `SPEC` declaration. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))
- **`getInstance`:** The source matches a one-argument call binding its sole argument to `protocol`, or a two-argument call binding the first argument to `protocol` and accepting any second argument (`_`). `protocol` is declared as `java.lang.String`; the second argument is not constrained in the event line. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))
- **`init`:** The source matches exactly the three-argument event `init(km, tm, random)`, with the declared object types shown above. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))
